question: Question linked to image nº17 A young patient of 22 years of age is referred to us from Primary Care. He is originally from Jamaica and has been living in Spain for five months. The reason for consulting the family doctor was a feeling of tiredness. As a background, he explains some pains of several years of evolution in various joints, of moderate intensity, without inflammatory signs, which had not been studied in his country. The clinical examination shows pale mucous membranes and a painful ulcerated lesion in the leg, of three years of evolution, for which he had not consulted. I did not remember any local trauma. The analytical sample shows a Hb of 7.6 g / dL, reticulocytes 417,000 / uL, Hto 22.8%, leukocytes 13.540 / uL, with 51% of neutrophils and 36% of lymphocytes, platelets 286,000 / uL, bilirubin 2.12 mg / dL, (direct 0.4 mg / dL) and lactate dehydrogenase 318 U / L (vn <190 U / L). A basic study of coagulation is within normal ranges. The chest radiograph is normal, as well as an Eco-Doppler of the lower extremities. What type of anemia would you suspect before starting the corresponding confirmatory studies?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Young patient from Jamaica" -> "high prevalence of sickle cell disease in Jamaica" -> "joint pains and leg ulcer" -> "symptoms consistent with sickle cell disease" -> "low Hb and high reticulocytes" -> "hemolytic anemia pattern" -> "elevated bilirubin and LDH" -> "suggests sickle cell anemia" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Pale mucous membranes" -> "anemia" -> "high reticulocyte count" -> "suggests hemolytic process" -> "elevated bilirubin and LDH" -> "hemolysis" -> "autoimmune hemolytic anemia possible" -> "but no evidence of autoimmune markers" -> "less likely autoimmune hemolytic anemia" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Chronic joint pain and leg ulcer" -> "chronic condition" -> "anemia of chronic disease possible" -> "but high reticulocytes and bilirubin" -> "not typical for anemia of chronic disease" -> "less likely anemia of chronic disease" -> 50%

CHAIN: "Pale mucous membranes" -> "anemia" -> "low Hb" -> "iron deficiency anemia possible" -> "but high reticulocytes and bilirubin" -> "not typical for iron deficiency anemia" -> "less likely iron deficiency anemia" -> 40%
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms and laboratory findings suggestive of hemolytic anemia. The low hemoglobin level, elevated reticulocyte count, and increased bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase levels indicate increased red blood cell turnover, consistent with hemolysis. The patient's Jamaican origin and the presence of a painful ulcerated lesion on the leg, which could be a leg ulcer associated with sickle cell disease, further support the suspicion of sickle cell anemia. Sickle cell disease is more prevalent in individuals of African descent and can cause chronic hemolytic anemia, joint pain, and leg ulcers. The normal coagulation study and absence of inflammatory signs make autoimmune hemolytic anemia and anemia of chronic disease less likely. Iron deficiency anemia typically presents with microcytic anemia and is less likely given the elevated reticulocyte count and bilirubin levels.
